query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of grain boundary-segregating elements can enhance room-temperature ductility in NbMoTaW without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy NbMoTaW
generation.intervention: Addition of grain boundary-segregating elements such as Boron
generation.mechanism: Reduced grain boundary embrittlement and enhanced dislocation mobility
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility without significant loss in high-temperature mechanical properties or irradiation resistance
generation.boundary: Elemental composition, processing conditions, and testing environments
generation.uncertainty: Optimal concentration of grain boundary-segregating elements and potential interactions with other alloying elements

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of grain boundary-segregating element concentrations and characterization of room-temperature ductility, high-temperature mechanical properties, and irradiation resistance
measurements: Tensile testing at room temperature and 1600 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of grain boundary-segregating elements does not improve room-temperature ductility or compromises high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified.
